title: Extract and test the Scaling page's derivations

Same treatment as the ICL page: move the pure logic to src/lib/ (compareArms, tallyGroups, totals, the floor-conditional, subsample) and pin every quoted number against the bundle.
close_reason: Done in 722b403: compareArms, tallyGroups, totals, the floor-conditional and subsample moved to src/lib/scaling.ts; Scaling.tsx 847 -> markup only. 87 new tests pin every quoted number against the bundle. Mutation-checked: TIE_MARGIN and MAX_RAW_POINTS each break 2-3 of them. 213 tests pass; typecheck, lint, build clean.

title: Add a render smoke test: boot the bundle and assert all 8 routes render
description: Every check this session was manual: start a server, click through, eyeball the console. The blank-page bug (App.tsx useMemo inside Async's render prop, React error #310) cost hours and would have been caught in seconds by an automated boot. Needs a test that builds, serves dist, loads the bundle headlessly, and asserts per-route: title renders, no .async__error, no .async__loading after settle, no NaN/undefined in text, and zero console errors. Note the existing test env is node-only (vitest, no jsdom installed) so this needs either jsdom+testing-library or a headless browser.

title: Reward.tsx lede claims the table 'cannot be reconstructed from released data'
description: Review MAJOR 1. It can: frontier_traj_reward.json ships per-round trajectories for all five ablation arms, and the page itself says so twice. The defensible narrower claim is that the training RUNS cannot be re-executed, only endpoints scored. The lede also contradicts the repo-wide derive-published-numbers rule.
close_reason: Fixed: the lede now says the training RUNS are what cannot be reconstructed, and that the per-round frontiers are released so endpoints are derivable.

title: Scaling.tsx: MAX_RAW_POINTS=1500 is dead; subsample's stride branch is unreachable
description: Review MINOR. Every ladder corpus has exactly 1,490 rows, so the 1,500 cap never triggers and the stride path at the subsample call site can never run. Lower the cap or simplify.
close_reason: Fixed: MAX_RAW_POINTS 1500 -> 1400, below the 1490 rows every ladder corpus carries, so the subsample stride path becomes reachable instead of dead.

The 116 float diffs (worst 4.3e-05) are all in unused fit params: 0 diffs in any frontier point and 0 diffs in any rendered string (alpha/rmse/bestLoss/nFrontier all identical; amplitude/floor differ only below the page's display precision). numpy-version noise, invisible to users. title: Reward.tsx: rowBest() and row.bestIndex disagree on the random-bytes row
description: Review MINOR 7. rowBest uses full precision and picks 'uniform' (8.0163 < 8.0204), shading the heatmap's alpha 0 off-best, while bestIndex encodes the paper's 2dp tie rule and bolds 'none' in the table. Two tables on one page disagree about the winner. Prefer bestIndex or round rowBest to 2dp. Latent too: build_data.py computes bestIndex over nulls-compacted rows but the page compares it to the column index -- safe only while no cell is null.
close_reason: Fixed: rowBest now compares at the table's printed 2dp, matching build_data.py's bestIndex, so the heatmap and the table agree on the random-bytes row.

title: Reward.tsx: 'shuffle is worse on 10 of 10' counts a printed tie as a loss
description: From the review. reward_arms.tex prints None, uniform AND shuffle all bold on the random-bytes row. Bundle: shuffle 8.0235 vs none 8.0204, delta 0.0031, so compareArms files it under 'worse'. Honest count is 9 worse + 1 tie. Also inconsistent with the page's own TIE_MARGIN=0.05 policy used on Scaling.
close_reason: Fixed: compareArms on Reward.tsx now has a TIE_EPS=0.005 bucket matching the tex's 2dp print precision, so shuffle reads 'worse on 9 of 10 (and ties it on 1: random bytes)' instead of 10/10.

title: Scaling.tsx: figure-2 arm compute axis does not match the authors' per-rung pools
description: From the review, and the most consequential data finding. tools/build_data.py effective_compute hardcodes P.POOL (1536) for all three arms, but the authors' fig2.py uses per-rung programs_per_round for the two fixed arms (prior: 1024/2048/1024/2048/1024; pcfg: 512/2048/2048/1024/1024). Recomputing with the authors' pools flips metamath from a tie to a pcfg win (3.064 vs 3.274) and moves every selfplay/pcfg loss in the table. The defect is in build_data.py, not the page, but the page asserts a fidelity the data lacks. Fix belongs upstream; needs a decision on scope.
close_reason: Fixed: arm_pool() in build_data.py reads the authors' per-rung *_programs_per_round.json for the two fixed arms (bundle key 'uniform' maps to file 'prior'); self-play stays at constant 1536. scaling.json regenerated. 13 new checks in verify_data.py recover the pool from C/(K*N*CTX*(r+1)) and assert selfplay=1536 constant and the others multi-valued; verified they fail (4 failures) when a constant pool is reintroduced. 165/165 pass.

title: Method.tsx: 'unmatched brackets are no-ops, which is what the paper specifies' is unsourced
description: Review M6. No artifact specifies no-op semantics. The behaviour is right and the page is forced into it -- the paper's own Table-1 Fibonacci program S,[[.C>.C>] has 1 unmatched bracket, and no-op treatment is what makes it emit 1,1,2,3,5,8. The wording should be 'as the paper's Table-1 programs require', not 'what the paper specifies'.
close_reason: Fixed: reworded to 'the reading the paper's own Table 1 programs require', noting its Fibonacci example has one unmatched bracket.

title: Method.tsx: preset note contradicts the step-limit caveat
description: Review MINOR/M2. At T=1024 the app's own geometric preset hits MAX_STEPS (stepLimited), and the page then says the paper would score it 'at the uniform-256 baseline of 8.0 bits/byte: nothing to learn'. Two errors: the program is highly structured, and 8.0 is this repo's uniform-256 baseline, not a paper measurement nor our 8.72 random-init control. Reword to say the truncation is ours and the sequence is truncated, not unlearnable.
close_reason: Fixed: the step-limit caveat no longer claims the paper would score the sequence at 8.0 bits/byte. It now says the output is truncated by this page's step guard, which is ours, and points at lowering T.
